joined to it by forks, either way), a view may show one of its mirrors
in its place. A perspective is one skgrepo, or the root homes, one per
tree: from a skgrepo, a node shows its mirror in that skgrepo, the node itself if it is homed there, else the
mirror in the skgrepo the config declares first. A fresh view is drawn
from its root homes: each tree from its root's home skgrepo,
throughout the tree, so a view of your note shows your mirrors where
your note's skgrepo holds them, and a view of someone else's note
shows theirs. That is the first perspective. The others are the
skgrepos home to a mirror of something the buffer shows whose
perspective would show some node of the buffer differently, each
followed in every tree, whatever its root's home, in the order the
config declares them, owned or foreign: so you can choose between a
private and a public fork of one note. After the last, the root homes
again. A skgrepo that would show the buffer as the root homes do is
skipped. The cycle is computed afresh at each switch, from what the
buffer shows then. A skgrepo is named by its label: "the perspective
of tracy".

Shown from your fork's skgrepo, a node of another's you fork there is
shown, after the save, as your clone. Shown from another skgrepo's,
a node you edit there is forked as anywhere, and the redraw shows
that skgrepo's version again, unedited, and the save says so; your
clone shows from your clone's skgrepo, unless that skgrepo holds the
original too, where the original stands. The redraw keeps the cursor and the folds.
The buffer keeps its perspective through its saves and the redraws
the server sends unasked. The switch is refused in a buffer of the
diff view, which shows no fork in place of what it forks,
and where no other perspective would show the buffer differently.
The roots are replaced too: from a skgrepo's perspective, a root with
a mirror in that skgrepo shows that mirror, standing where the root
stood, with the cursor still on it if it was, and with its own
folders, as a fresh view of it would draw them (its containers, its
forks folder and count, and any other folder you had opened there);
from the root homes, the node you opened, as it is. The buffer keeps its name. In a search
buffer, the hits are its roots. See =docs/mirrors.org=.

Emacs names any perspective but the root homes in the mode name:
"SKG:the perspective of tracy". The Neovim client draws no statusline of its
own; the buffer keeps the perspective in 'b:skg_perspective'
and its name in 'b:skg_perspective_name', and
=%{v:lua.require'skg.buffer'.perspective_mode_line()}= in
your 'statusline' (or 'winbar') shows ":the perspective of tracy", say, in such
a view and nothing elsewhere.
*** <localleader>vr : :SkgReadableIdsToggle
This changes how node IDs are displayed.
The ID itself is a kind of special random gibberish called UUID v4.
When ReadableIdsToggle is on,
only the first 8 characters of the ID are shown (the rest is
concealed to an ellipsis, though the underlying text -- and
copy-paste -- still has the full ID),
and they are followed by the title of the node with that ID,
if Skg can figure it out. It works in .skg file buffers and in
git-status / git-diff buffers alike, but the key is bound only in
content views: elsewhere, run ':SkgReadableIdsToggle'. A .skg file
buffer starts with it on.
(It doesn't yet know how to read the git history
to find titles for deleted files.)
*** <localleader>vR : :SkgReadableIdsRefresh
The ID-to-title map is cached for the whole Neovim session, so a
neogit refresh re-requests nothing it has already seen. This empties
the cache and annotates the current buffer again. Use it after
anything that changes what titles the server would answer with: a
node retitled, or a skgrepo widening (IDs restricted under the old
skgrepo restriction were cached as unresolvable). The key is bound in
content views only; elsewhere, run ':SkgReadableIdsRefresh'.
*** <localleader>vs : :SkgViewLinkstack
View and maybe edit the set of links you've stored.
(See "the linkstack" below.)
*** <localleader>vu : :SkgToggleForkDedupOverlay
Toggles, in this buffer, the extmarks that cover what a member of a
forks folder restates of its note, as C-c v u does in Emacs: =<b's
title, unchanged>= over a title equal to the note's, =<b's body,
unchanged>= over such a body, its other lines concealed. They are on
unless the buffer variable 'skg_fork_dedup_overlay' is false. The
buffer always holds the real text, and a save sends it.
*** <localleader>vw : :SkgViewWithoutMetadata
If a Visual-mode selection is active (or was just left, via the
='<,'>= marks), opens a new org buffer containing that region,
but with the '(skg ...)' metadata stripped from every headline.
Otherwise it does nothing.
This is useful for copying a read-only projection of some data
into another application.
** <localleader>{i|u|o} : IDs, links and the linkstack
*** some background
**** IDs are mostly invisible, but good to know about.
Every node has an ID,
which you can see if you disable heralds ('HeraldsToggle',
<localleader>vh).
Every link also has an ID and a label,
but all you see when you look at the ID is the label,
unless you disable org-mode (say, by switching to text-mode).
You should never need to see IDs explicitly.
**** The linkstack
is, like it sounds, a stack of links.
A stack is just a list that you interact with,
mostly from one side, the 'top':
You can 'push' something onto the top of the stack,
and you can 'pop' something off of the top of the stack.
But you can also jump to a view of your entire stack,
using (copying, pasting, deleting) it
without any restrictions on order.
*** ]i (also <localleader>in) : :SkgIdNext
Makes the cursor hop among two kinds of IDs:
The ID associated with a node in the view,
and the ID associated with a link in a node's title.
Every node has an ID,
but a title can include multiple or no links.
*** [i (also <localleader>ip) : :SkgIdPrev
See IdNext, above.
*** the linkstack
<localleader>u for push, <localleader>o _ for paste,
<localleader>O _ for pop.

Inside a Vim command-line prompt (search, an Ex command's argument,
...), <localleader> chords aren't available, so paste and pop also
ride cmdline-mode mappings: <C-x>i pastes the top id, <C-x>l pastes
a link to it, <C-x>I pops the id, <C-x>L pops the link. (Push, and
pasting/popping a full node, have no cmdline form -- do those from
a buffer.)
**** <localleader>u : :SkgIdPush
Stores, in the linkstack,
a link to the node the cursor is on.
**** <localleader>oi : :SkgPasteId
Inserts the ID at the top of the linkstack at the cursor.
Does not modify the stack.
**** <localleader>Oi : :SkgPopId
Like PasteId,
but also removes the node from the stack.
**** <localleader>ol : :SkgPasteLink
Inserts, at the cursor, a link to the node
whose ID is at the top of the linkstack.
Does not modify the stack.
**** <localleader>Ol : :SkgPopLink
Like PasteLink,
but also removes the node from the stack.
**** <localleader>on : :SkgPasteNode
This is the easiest way to give a node multiple containers --
push it to the stack, then paste it as a node somewhere else.

Inserts, at the cursor, a write-protected view
of the node whose ID is at the top of the linkstack.
Its metadata includes only the ID, =writeProtected=,
and (usually) an editable view request;
its title comes from the stack.
Does not modify the stack or save.
Saving will provide the rest of its metadata,
and fulfill the editable view request,
making the node writable with its real title, body and content.

The view request is omitted if the buffer already has
an editable occurrence of the node (or one requesting an editable view),
because a buffer can hold only one editable occurrence of each node.
Then the pasted node stays write-protected, and Neovim says so.
**** <localleader>On : :SkgPopNode
Like PasteNode,
but also removes the node from the stack.
**** <localleader>vs : :SkgViewLinkstack
repeated here; described earlier in this doc
** keys outside content views
Most keys above are bound only in a content view, a buffer showing
part of the graph. A few work elsewhere; every ':Skg' command works
anywhere.
- In a buffer reading a .skg file: <localleader>gg and
  <localleader>GG, ]i and [i (also <localleader>in and
  <localleader>ip), and the linkstack's paste and pop keys
  (<localleader>oi, ol, on, Oi, Ol, On).
- In a read-only report (an unknown graphnode's investigation, the import
  result): <localleader>ff and fi, the <localleader>g / G keys but
  gb and gv, <localleader>ve, vl and vs, <localleader>in and ip, and
  the linkstack keys (<localleader>u, oi, ol, on, Oi, Ol, On).
- In a command-line prompt: <C-x>i, <C-x>l, <C-x>I and <C-x>L (see
  "the linkstack").
- In the metadata editor (<localleader>vm): ':w' or <localleader>cc
  applies the edit, and S-Left / S-Right cycle a field's value.
- In the fork-confirmation buffer: <localleader>cc approves and
  <localleader>ck declines.
** buffer mechanics with no Emacs-chord counterpart
These are defined directly in =attach_content_view=
(nvim/lua/skg/keymaps.lua) rather than translated from a =C-c=
chord: they ride keys nvim already gives special meaning to.
*** <Tab> : toggle the fold at point
Equivalent to org's own =za=: opens or closes the fold under the
cursor.
*** <S-Tab> : toggle global fold visibility
All folds closed <-> all folds open, buffer-wide.
*** ^ : :SkgBeginningOfLine
Toggles the cursor between the start of the line and the start of
the title (the text after the stars and any =(skg ...)= metadata).
The nvim analog of the Emacs client's C-a toggle. On a
non-headline, it's just beginning-of-line.
*** cit / ciT : cycle the TODO keyword
Cycles the headline's TODO keyword forward (=cit=) or backward
(=ciT=) without corrupting its metadata: the =(skg ...)= sexp is
stripped before org's own TODO-cycling runs, then re-inserted
after the stars and before the (possibly new) keyword.
** importing Markdown and Org
*** :SkgImportMdAndOrg
With the server running, choose an absolute input directory in the
server/container filesystem and an existing owned destination skgrepo. The
skgrepo determines the privacy of all new nodes; one the
skgrepo restriction keeps out is refused. Skg scans exact =.md= and
=.org= files recursively, leaves the originals untouched, and asks for a
host-root mapping only when absolute links to =.md= or =.org= files occur.
Blank mapping leaves unresolved links with warnings. Links to other kinds of
files are left pointing where they did, without warnings. Review the file/node counts, generated
export paths, and diagnostics; then explicitly confirm or decline. A changed
input or destination requires a fresh preview.

The import is additive: it creates file-root and headline nodes, an import
record, and an Org export marker under each file root. The import result
buffer links to the record; follow it with =<localleader>gg=. A document whose
only top-level headline has nothing before it uses that headline as its
file root; otherwise the file root, titled after the document, holds the
text before the first headline, and its export marker's
=root_headline = false= makes the document export with its original
outline. Org links to non-document files stay as written. It does not replace
existing =.skg= files, copy attachments, synchronize later changes, or export
automatically. Most original markup remains text; Markdown hard breaks become
Org's two-backslash form so save-time trailing-whitespace cleanup remains.
Later export is a readable rendition, not a round-trip backup. Exporting to
the original directory overwrites matching =.org= files but not =.md= files.
There is no dedicated undo or crash-recovery transaction.

In Org files, link syntax inside text Org shows literally (=verbatim=,
~code~, a fixed-width line beginning with =: =, a =#+begin_...= block, or a
=```= fence) is an example, and is left alone; backticks are not literal in
Org. A line that looks like an Org headline inside a block or fence stops the
import, with nothing written; close the block, or escape the line with a
leading comma (=,* ...=). The Emacs command reference explains both in more
detail.
** exporting to org
*** :SkgExportToOrg
Exports Skg data to plain =.org= files, so the data can be read
(and navigated on GitHub) without running Skg. No keybinding.
It ignores the connection's skgrepo restriction: what it exports is
decided by the most private skgrepo it asks for, below, whatever
':SkgRestrictRepoSet' (<localleader>vl) chose.
Each file begins with comments naming its source node's ID and warning
that direct edits will be clobbered by the next export; the importer
ignores them.

It asks two things:
- which skgrepo-set to export, as the most private owned skgrepo to
  export (command-line input with TAB completion and S-Left /
  S-Right cycling); only nodes from that set, and from the foreign
  skgrepos, are included. Choose a
  public-facing skgrepo so private notes are not exported; exporting
  the most private skgrepo (no skgrepo restriction) warns you about
  this.
- which directory to write to (default =org-exports=). This path
  is interpreted *by the server*, relative to the project root the
  server runs from. Because the server may run inside a Docker
  container whose filesystem differs from the host running Neovim,
  this prompt has no path completion. An absolute path is used
  as-is.

If a restricted export would include overPrivateText telescope text, Skg asks for
request-scoped approval before writing any file. An export of the
most private skgrepo (no skgrepo restriction) includes it with a warning. The noninteractive form fails closed unless passed
=--include-overPrivateText-telescopes=:

: cargo run --bin skg -- export-org [config-path] [skgrepo-restriction] [output-dir] [--include-overPrivateText-telescopes]

A node is exported when one of its children, an export marker
('docs/glossary.org', "export root, export marker"), has a title
linking to the export instruction node and a body giving a
=target_filepath= (TOML-ish: =target_filepath = docs/setup=,
quoted if it contains whitespace). That parent is written to
=<output-dir>/<target_filepath>.org= as a recursive content view,
stripped of skg metadata. The export marker is omitted. If the
marker's body also says =root_headline = false=, the parent's title is
not a headline: its body opens the file, and its children are the
top-level headlines.

Links are rewritten to relative org links, except examples in text
Org shows literally (verbatim, code, fixed-width lines, blocks and
fences). A link to another
exported file's root points at that file; a link to a non-root
node points deep, via =[[./file.org::*Headline][label]]=, or via
=[[./file.org::#ID][label]]= when that headline contains a link
or repeats an earlier headline's text in its file
(the headline then gets a =:CUSTOM_ID: ID= property), or via the
=CUSTOM_ID= of a property drawer that begins the headline's body. A
link labeled with its own destination (=file:file.org=) is exported
unlabeled. A nested
export root is shown as a link, not inlined. A link whose dest
is not exported under the chosen set points to the export of the
node "Some links might be broken.", or, when that node is not
exported either, becomes its plain label.

Existing files in the output dir are overwritten in place; other
files there are left untouched.
** connection, reload, rebuild session-lifetime stores
Unless you're coding or troubleshooting,
you probably won't need these.
*** :SkgInit CONFIG-PATH
Initializes the client against a skgconfig.toml.
*** :SkgConnectionVerify
Sends a ping to the Rust server
to check if the connection is working.
Displays the result in the echo area.
*** :SkgConnectionEnd
Closes the TCP connection to the Rust server.
*** :SkgRebuildSessionLifetimeStores
Re-reads the config file and the authoritative =.skg= files, validates and
replaces the in-memory graph, and rebuilds the derived Tantivy search index.
It does not rewrite the =.skg= files. So an edited config (a skgrepo added,
removed or reordered, say) takes effect without restarting the server, except
for its 'port' and 'timing_log', which the answer warns about. An invalid
config fails the rebuild, and the server keeps serving the old one.
After a successful rebuild every view without unsaved edits is
rerendered from the rebuilt graph, as ':SkgRerenderAllViews' does; the
views with unsaved edits are named and left as they are, and a save of
one is checked like any other. Files that change on disk need no
rebuild: the server reloads them as they change (see the start of this
document).
*** :SkgStripBodyWhitespace
Strips trailing whitespace from every line of every body,
in every skgrepo you own.
Foreign skgrepos are never written, so they are left untouched.
It ignores the skgrepo restriction: it rewrites the bodies of nodes
the skgrepo restriction keeps out too.
Rewrites exactly the .skg files whose bodies change;
the derived caches are refreshed to match.
Open views stay valid: their saves are not refused for it.
*** :SkgCloseAllSkgBuffers
Kills every skg view buffer (each triggers a close-view notice to
the server first).
*** :SkgReload
Unloads all skg Lua modules and reloads them from disk.
Useful when you've changed Lua code
and want to pick up the changes without restarting Neovim.
